title: a word for wishing well on people you don't like
hookLine: a word for wishing well on people you don't like

cards: The coworker who replies all. The neighbor with the leaf blower at seven on a Saturday. The relative with opinions about your life at every holiday.
Not villains. Just people who are hard to like. Maybe a face comes to mind already.
Now here's an old Buddhist practice: people sit quietly and wish that person well. On purpose. Not because they've forgiven anything, and not because the person has earned it.
Just as training, the way you'd train a muscle. It sounds almost backwards. Buddhists trace it to the Buddha's own teaching.

teach.b: Metta. It's a word in Pali, the old language the Buddha's teachings were kept in. It comes from mitta, a friend.
So metta is friendliness. A wish for someone's good, the plain warm kind you'd feel for a friend, pointed at anyone at all.
You may know its Sanskrit cousin, maitri, or the name Maitreya, the friendly one, the Buddha that tradition says is still to come.
There's a short teaching on it, the Metta Sutta, still chanted in Buddhist homes and monasteries.

teach.h: LIKE A MOTHER WITH HER ONLY CHILD.
teach.b: It pictures a mother protecting her only child with her own life, and says to hold a heart like that toward every living being. Seen and unseen. Near and far.
Born and not yet born. Every one.
And the Buddha's own verses put the reason bluntly: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." An old rule. Not a new idea even then.
How do people actually do it? Later teachers laid out a gentle order.

teach.h: YOU, A FRIEND, A STRANGER, THE HARD ONE.
teach.b: Start with yourself, because it's hard to give what you've never felt. Then someone you love. Then someone neutral, the person who sells you coffee.
Then, last and slowest, someone difficult. You don't pretend to like them.

You just wish them what you'd want: to be safe, to be well, to be at ease. Some who practice it describe an odd side effect: it changes them more than anyone else. The difficult person is still difficult.
They just carry less of that person around.

how: Buddhists practice metta by silently repeating short wishes, such as may you be safe, may you be well, may you be at ease, first for themselves and then outward to loved ones, strangers, difficult people and all beings; the Metta Sutta is chanted in monasteries and homes.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: a mother with her only child
the picture of how wide it goes

s: metta means you have to like everyone
it's a wish for someone's good. you don't have to like them, or pretend to.
metta comes from the Pali word for friend
mitta, a friend. metta is friendliness, pointed at anyone.
the Buddha's verses call "hatred ceases by love" a new idea

games.q: you're learning metta the traditional way. who do you start with?
o: the most difficult person you know.
games.why: the classic order, set out by the commentator Buddhaghosa, starts with yourself, then a loved one, then a stranger, and only then someone difficult. the hard one comes last, and slowly.

practice: The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Start where the old order starts: with yourself. Breathe in, and on the way out let a few words go: may I be at ease.
Then someone you love: may you be at ease. Then a stranger, the person who sells you coffee. Then, if you're ready, that face from a minute ago.
You don't have to feel warm. Just let the words go out, one breath at a time.

wordCard.voice: Metta. Friendliness. A wish for anyone's good, even the people who make it hard. Fifteenth word.

orig.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: friendliness, goodwill. From mitta, a friend. Sanskrit: maitrī.

carryVoice: Your line: may you be at ease. You don't have to like someone to wish them well. Day fifteen.
